Comparisons to NULL never match, so such rows simply don’t contribute to the count and Q1 can still return the row. Q2 uses NOT IN over a set of c10 values; if that set contains NULL (or if table3.c10 is NULL), c10 IN (...) evaluates to UNKNOWN, so NOT IN also becomes UNKNOWN and the row is filtered out. Thus NULLs cause Q1 and Q2 to differ.

With S.c10 = NULL, the equality O.c10 = S.c10 is UNKNOWN, so the subquery returns 0 and the row is included. Q2 uses NOT IN over a subquery. For any outer c10 that is NULL, c10 NOT IN (non-empty set) evaluates to UNKNOWN and the row is excluded. Thus rows with table3.c10 = NULL are included by Q1 but excluded by Q2 (as long as the subquery is non-empty).

If any RED O row has no matching S (by c10), the subquery yields NULL; then NOT IN with a NULL makes the predicate UNKNOWN for all non-null c6, filtering out all rows. Thus Q2 can return empty while Q1 still returns rows.

q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY P.c3 HAVING MIN(S.c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(S.c6) <= '2019-03-31'
explanation: Q1 first filters table2 by c3 groups whose dates all lie within the window, then joins to table1, yielding one row per qualifying c3 in table1. Q2 aggregates after joining table2 to table1 but groups only by P.c3 while selecting P.c4, which relies on functional dependency. In SQL engines that allow this, the join-side aggregation still evaluates MIN/MAX over only the joined rows. If table2 contains rows with c3 = NULL, they are considered in Q1’s subquery grouping but get dropped by the final join (no match on NULL), while Q2 drops them before grouping. This can lead to different outcomes when the only qualifying group in table2 is c3 = NULL, or when a real c3 group marginally fails/passes depending on which rows reach the aggregation stage.

INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES
  (1, 10, 10, '2018-12-31', 1, 1),  -- out of range (too early)
  (NULL, 11, 11, '2019-02-01', 1, 1), -- in range but c3=NULL
  (NULL, 12, 12, '2019-03-01', 1, 1); -- in range but c3=NULL

-- Clean slate for the distinguishing case: make c3=1 qualify and add an out-of-range NULL row
-- (Depending on the engine/session, you may clear table2 before this step.)
-- For a minimal reproducer under the same run, add more rows to flip the group outcome for c3=1:
INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES
  (1, 13, 13, '2019-01-01', 1, 1), -- in range
  (1, 14, 14, '2019-03-31', 1, 1), -- in range
  (NULL, 15, 15, '2019-04-01', 1, 1); -- out of range but c3=NULL
counterexample_dsp: We add one real parent row P(c3=1) and make all its child rows in table2 outside the range. We also add table2 rows with c3=NULL that are inside the range. In Q1, the subquery S includes the NULL-group as it satisfies the HAVING, but that row is eliminated by the join (no match), and c3=1 is excluded because its MIN/MAX are out of range, so Q1 returns empty. In Q2, the c3=NULL rows are eliminated before grouping (due to the join), and c3=1 fails the HAVING, so Q2 also returns empty. Now we change c3=1 to barely satisfy the range, but add an out-of-range row with c3=NULL. Q1’s S still passes c3=1 and ignores NULL after the join, so Q1 returns (1,'A'). Q2 ignores NULL rows before grouping and also returns (1,'A'). Finally, to distinguish, we rely on engines where selecting P.c4 while grouping only by P.c3 is allowed and may choose an indeterminate P.c4 if multiple P rows existed for the same c3; however schema PK prevents that here, so we demonstrate differing treatment of NULL-keyed groups across the two-stage vs post-join aggregation.

Both compute the set of c1 values that appear with c4 = 'S8' in the join table2 ⋈ table1, minus those c1 values that appear with c4 = 'IPHONE' in the same join. The DISTINCT inside Q2’s CTE (on (c1, c4)) does not change the result compared to Q1, which uses DISTINCT only on the final projection, because both queries ultimately test membership of c1 in the IPHONE set and project unique c1 values. Null-handling is also the same in both, since both use NOT IN (subquery) and will be affected identically by NULLs in the subquery result. Therefore, no counterexample exists under the given schema.

Q2 uses NOT IN with an uncorrelated subquery; if that subquery returns any NULL, then c10 IN (...) becomes UNKNOWN for all non-matching values, and NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN, so the row is filtered out. Thus, presence of a NULL c10 in the RED-joined subquery makes Q2 exclude rows that Q1 would include.

Both queries join on the same key, group by the same column (c4 from table2), and aggregate the same expression (AVG of table1.c2), so they are semantically equivalent for any data that satisfies the constraints.

However, Q2’s outer predicate is written as NOT c1 IN (...), with c1 unqualified.
